headline: As the author of the “Iskander-1000” designation, the MilitaryRussia project felt the need to comment on the information released by Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence (GUR/HUR) about its alleged first use against targets in Ukraine. The claim is based on the discovery of missile remnants bearing the 9M723-2 designation. Here’s the important part: 1. 9M723-2 and 9M723-2F3 are NOT the “Iskander-1000” with an extended range. This comes down to how Soviet/Russian missile designations work. The 9M723 designation refers to the missile/rocket section, while the warhead has its own designation. Different warheads can be fitted to the same missile section. For example, the 9M723K5 consists of the 9M723 missile section fitted with the 9N722K5 warhead. Information available from 2011 mentioned two missile-section variants: 9M723 and 9M723-1. A new version, provisionally designated 9M723-2, appeared in 2024. MilitaryRussia initially used the 9M723-2 designation in 2024 to identify what it called the “Iskander-1000”, a proposed extended-range version of the Iskander. They now consider that identification to have been incorrect. Based on the available information, the more likely breakdown is: • 9M723 — an earlier missile section with a clearly visible cable channel along the body. • 9M723-1 — a more conventional design, with six decoys located in the rear section. • 9M723-2 — a newer design without the six decoys, but with additional antenna modules associated with the satellite-navigation system. 2. What about the reported 800 km launch? On December 18, 2025, Ukrainian media reported a missile launch to a range of around 800 km. MilitaryRussia believes this may have been a test launch of the actual “Iskander-1000” using the standard Iskander launcher. 3. So what exactly is the 9M723-2? At this point, there are two main possibilities. It could be a simplified and lighter version of the 9M723-1 of the 9K720 “Iskander-M” system. Also, it could be a newer version designed to provide better accuracy and greater resistance to electronic warfare. For now, this is still speculation. The secrecy surrounding new Russian missile developments, combined with the lack of clear photographic evidence from the crash sites, means there is not enough information to draw firm conclusions.

headline: The Maritime Administration (MARAD) has activated SUNY Maritime College’s training ship Empire State VII for temporary federal service beginning around Sept. 1, according to the college. MARAD has given the vessel a notional mission duration of approximately 170 days, but has not publicly disclosed the mission or destination. The Maritime Executive reports that Diego Garcia is rumored as a possible destination, although that has not been confirmed. The activation is notable because Empire State is the first National Security Multi-Mission Vessel (NSMV) to be activated for federal service. However, the use of training ships for federal missions is not unprecedented. Earlier vessels in the Empire State training-ship lineage, including Empire State VI, have previously been activated for federal service in support of government missions. The new Empire State was specifically designed with government missions in mind and can accommodate roughly 600 people, with capacity for up to 1,000, along with a full hospital. Those capabilities make the NSMV suitable for humanitarian assistance, logistics, evacuation or other government requirements. The timing is particularly notable because the ship had only returned to New York on July 16 after a two-month international training cruise and was beginning the new academic year. Approximately 400 incoming students had recently arrived and begun their training aboard the vessel. Source: https://maritime-executive.com/article/marad-calls-up-training-ship-empire-state-for-federal-service

headline: The Department of War has confirmed that at least seven U.S. military commissaries have reported refrigeration problems this week, including facilities at Fort Irwin, Holloman AFB, Naval Station Newport, Little Rock AFB, F.E. Warren AFB, Robins AFB and Fort Huachuca. The below photos were posted by Fort Irwin to social media. The disruptions have resulted in some stores restricting sales to dry goods, while refrigerated and frozen products have been removed or discarded. Fort Huachuca reported that all frozen food was spoiled after freezers entered defrost mode. DoW says the Defense Commissary Agency is moving products to alternate temperature-controlled locations and taking precautions to prevent further losses and ensure food safety. The cause remains unknown. Some online speculation has suggested a coordinated cyberattack or deliberate disruption of network connected refrigeration systems, but there is currently no official evidence presented in the article supporting that explanation. DoD specifically declined to speculate on the cause or say whether the outages are being investigated as a connected incident. headline: CIA Director Visit to Russia, Reasons, and Forecast (General Access) ICOD-1110, 08/28/2026 BLUF: On Tuesday, August 25, 2026, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise visit to Russia to meet with his Russian counterpart, Russian Foreign Intelligence Service Director Sergei Naryshkin. While Russian news and official outlets characterized the meeting as 'contacts' with their U.S. intelligence counterparts, declining to elaborate on what was said, amidst increased Russian hybrid and direct actions against European nations, U.S. news outlets were told by U.S. and European officials that the meeting was set to warn Russia against attacking a NATO partner, urge them to reenter Russo-Ukrainian peace talks, and distance themselves from Iran. This has prompted many to double down on reports that Russia may have been planning a direct military action against a NATO member state in the near term. Key Points: - U.S. President Donald J. Trump personally dispatched Director Ratcliffe to Russia, keeping both his counterparts in Europe and some top U.S. officials and administration aides in the dark on the matter. This caused a general scramble of diplomatic communications and wider speculation when Ratcliffe's C-17 was seen flying into Russia. - Intelligence suggested that Russia may have been preparing a direct, albeit limited, action against ba NATO member state. - Two primary rundowns of what was communicated to Russia have come out: • That NATO Article 5 commitments remain robust (in effect warning Russia against attacking a NATO member state), that Russo-Ukrainian peace/ceasefire processes should be restarted, and that Russia must distance itself from Iran. • That the primary purpose of the meeting was to communicate Russia's inability to decisively win a largely stalemated war with Ukraine. (various casualty, industry, and other metrics were reportedly cited.) - Hybrid actions indirectly attributed to the Russians and/or directly traced to them have increased notably in the past months with a number of notable incidents, including a potential clandestine sabotage mission against a German military facility, stopped by Serbian authorities; cyberwarfare activities against France; and numerous drones shot down and drone impacts in both Romania and the Baltics. - ISR was increasingly active around the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad in the days/week leading up to the visit. Analyst Comment Additional reports that Russian President Vladimir Putin may be pushed to execute a limited tactical nuclear strike have been factored into this assessment but do not weigh heavily on our I&W tree. Assessment: The aforementioned dynamic, coupled with the largely stalemated battlefield dynamic of the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian War, has led some to believe that, seeking to implement an 'escalate to deescalate' strategy, Russian President Vladimir Putin may be looking to escalate against NATO as a means to cause a fracture within NATO and possibly expose NATO's Article 5 defense clause as largely a bluff, which would in turn aid in his primary venture of the war in Ukraine. As mentioned in the "Key Points" portion of this assessment, there are two prevailing characterizations of the intelligence meeting on the 25th, but that does not mean both cannot be true at the same time, as the Trump administration has been keen to publicly isolate Iran economically and diplomatically and realize a U.S.-brokered settlement of the Russo-Ukrainian War, while simultaneously, Russian actions against NATO member states have been increasing. Additionally, the meeting this past week with the policy heads of NATO member states, including U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby, where key new and to-be-renewed NATO force model and policy frameworks were set to be discussed, also likely plays some part in the timing of the meeting. Key Judgement: - It's currently highly unlikely that Russia is seeking to use tactical nuclear weapons on the battlefield in Ukraine in the near-term, as Russian tactical nuclear use, from a doctrinal perspective, is meant to forestall a significant collapse of Russian forces on the battlefield, something that is not currently happening. - A Russian attack on a NATO member state is currently unlikely in the near-term, as Russian readiness is not currently at a level to withstand the potential NATO response should Article 5 be implemented. Additionally, per Western news outlets, Baltic intelligence agencies currently assess the likelihood of such a move by Russia against them in the near-term as low. - As assessed in previous assessments, barring significant concessions, it's still unlikely that Russian president Vladimir Putin will seriously reenter talks to end the ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war. - Barring a more robust European response to Russian hybrid actions, it's unlikely that a warning alone, even that from the CIA director, will avert Russia from its current course of action as it relates to grey-zone operations against nations that support Ukraine. END

headline: During his recent mysterious visit to Moscow, CIA Director John Ratcliffe proposed a trilateral summit between President Trump, Russian President Putin and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy during a covert meeting with SVR Foreign Intelligence Chief Sergey Naryshkin and FSB Director Alexander Bortnikov, two sources briefed on the matter have told Axios. Ratcliffe’s visit was partly aimed at determining whether Russia’s heads of intelligence services could help convince Putin to move toward resuming negotiations aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine War. During the meeting, Ratcliffe gave Bortnikov “a bleak assessment” of the state of the war and urged Russia to cut a deal with Ukraine and the United States. On Friday, U.S. officials briefed Zelenskyy on Ratcliffe’s talks in Moscow and the proposal for a trilateral summit, an idea which he had previously supported, though has been continually rejected by Putin. Reports by local media in Ukraine has suggested that negotiations could resume in September.

headline: China is rapidly expanding the Lop Nur flight test complex in Xinjiang, a highly restricted facility used for testing advanced and experimental military aircraft. Lop Nur has previously been associated with testing China's J-36 and J-XDS sixth generation fighter designs. The latest construction is particularly notable because the new southern hangars are substantially wider than typical tactical-aircraft shelters. The War Zone assesses that the facilities could eventually support larger aircraft, including China's H-20 stealth bomber, which has yet to publicly appear. However, the article emphasizes that there is currently no evidence the H-20 is headed to Lop Nur, making that an assessment rather than a confirmed development. The broader takeaway is that Lop Nur is evolving from a relatively austere test airfield into a major, high capacity test center for China's next generation aerospace programs, with the pace of construction accelerating significantly in 2025–26. Source: https://www.twz.com/news-features/chinas-area-51-is-undergoing-a-massive-expansion

headline: Ukraine has received intelligence that Russia is planning a new ground offensive from Belarus against the capital of Kyiv and Chernihiv, while Moscow ramps up drone and missile strikes on cities throughout Ukraine, according to a report by POLITICO. Speaking Saturday to reporters, Pavlo Palisa, the Deputy Head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, said that Russian military leadership had been tasked by the Kremlin with planning and preparing for attacks on the two cities, via intelligence received and verified by Ukraine’s Main Directorate of Intelligence. So far, Palisa states, evidence does not suggest that Russian ground forces are massing in Belarus and Western Russia for such an operation, but that Ukraine’s priority is to “prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to launch any offensive actions at all.” At the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Russian ground forces attempted an offensive on Kyiv, launched in part from nearby Belarus, but ultimately became bogged down due to strikes on logistics lines before being crushed and repelled by the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
